report.summary: Chunk 5 of session.py: council execution loop with floor refusal, budget rounds, token ceiling, and turn recording; helpers for turn refs and chain reading.
risks: _first_offending_path | medium | The function imports secret_floor_rule from sensitivity module which is not shown; if that module behaves unexpectedly, the floor check could miss paths. | Review the secret_floor_rule implementation in the sensitivity module.

handoff.purpose: Implements the main council execution loop including floor refusal, token ceiling enforcement, round dispatch, and budget rounds; defines helper functions for turn creation and chain reading.

symbols.name: _first_offending_path
symbols.note: Returns the first evidence path that triggers the secret floor rule, or empty string if none.

symbols.name: _unavailable_turn
symbols.note: Creates a turn dict for an unavailable adapter (timeout or transport error).

symbols.name: _append_budget_round
symbols.note: Records a budget-exhausted round for all seated adapters.

symbols.name: _chained
symbols.note: Reads this round's turns from the chain (load_transcript).

symbols.name: _turn_ref
symbols.note: Constructs a TurnRef from a turn id and chain record.

claims.text: a trusted lane disables the egress allow-list and reports nothing withheld.
claims.why: The claim about trusted lane behavior is in a ValueError message; the actual logic for trusted lanes is not in this chunk.

claims.text: PRE-FLIGHT SECRET FLOOR. Per path, per file, never over the assembled prompt: the path tier is the only thing that catches a patch which ADDS `.env`, and a concatenated scan kills it. A hit refuses the whole council -- there is no redact-and-send -- and NO VENDOR IS CALLED.
claims.why: The comment describes behavior of floor_check and the refusal process; the actual floor_check function is not defined in this chunk.

claims.text: Charge the token ceiling BEFORE dispatch, from the assembled prompt. Reconciling after the call is not a budget.
claims.why: The code at lines 1180-1184 checks token_ceiling before dispatching and charges tokens_charged accordingly.

claims.text: Hung or crashed: recorded as a turn, never as an absence.
claims.why: Code at lines 1197-1201 creates a turn via _unavailable_turn when reply is None.

claims.text: Nobody had a voice this round; another round would prompt on an empty transcript and pretend to be a deliberation.
claims.why: Code at lines 1238-1240 breaks the loop with ended='no_voice' if no actor spoke.

claims.text: A blown wall clock is NOT handled here: the next iteration's top-of-round check records a budget_exhausted turn per participant first. Breaking early would shorten the council silently.
claims.why: The loop continues to next iteration where the top-of-round check (line 1170) records budget rounds if remaining <= 0.

claims.text: A blown budget is a RECORDED round, not a shortened one.
claims.why: The function creates a batch of turns for all seated adapters and appends them as a round.

claims.text: Read this round's turns back FROM THE CHAIN. Round 2 prompts are built from these, not from the in-memory replies: a turn the secret floor refused is a receipt on disk, and re-feeding the raw reply would smuggle the refused bytes into another vendor's prompt.
claims.why: The claim about how prompts are built and the security implication refers to code outside this chunk (e.g., _round_body).

observations.what: The function _first_offending_path imports secret_floor_rule inside the function body, which may cause repeated imports if called many times.

In the main loop, the variable 'prior' is built from chained records (line 1236) and used in _round_body (line 1178). This ensures that only persisted turns are fed back, as per the _chained docstring.
The variable 'floor_rule' is set from refusal.rule (line 1160) and also updated from ref.reason when status is 'refused' (line 1233). This ensures floor_rule captures the first refusal reason.

The code uses time.monotonic() for deadline and started, but does not account for time spent in floor_check or other operations before the loop. The wall_clock_s measurement includes the entire function after seating.

The token_ceiling check uses tokens_charged + per_call_tokens > token_ceiling (line 1184). If token_ceiling is very large, this could overflow if tokens_charged is large, but Python integers are arbitrary precision so no overflow.
